after.summary:
Between 16 October and 4 November 2026, the United States of America, through its International Health Regulations (IHR) National Focal Point, notified WHO of three laboratory-confirmed human infections with influenza A(H5) virus in Washington State. These included one fatal case, the first reported death following exposure to infected dairy cattle or a related contaminated environment. All three cases were adults who worked on dairy cattle farms in Yakima County, Washington State, where the highly pathogenic (in animals) avian influenza (HPAI) A(H5N1) virus had recently been detected in dairy cattle. 
Investigations and monitoring of exposed people and close contacts are ongoing. Based on information available to date, there is no evidence of human-to-human transmission.

In accordance with the IHR (2005), any human infection caused by a new influenza A virus subtype is considered a potentially significant public health event and is subject to mandatory notification to WHO. Based on the information currently available on this and previous cases, WHO assesses the risk to the general population posed by A(H5N1) viruses as low. For individuals with occupational exposure to these viruses, the risk of infection is considered low to moderate. The situation may change as more information becomes available. 
WHO continues to closely monitor these viruses and the global epidemiological situation.

In October 2026, a cluster of four cases of acute flaccid paralysis (AFP) was identified in Al-Mayadin District, Deir Ez Zor Governorate, Syrian Arab Republic. As of 13 November 2026, three confirmed cases of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 1 (cVDPV1) have been reported. Vaccine-derived poliovirus type 1 (VDPV1) was also detected in three contacts who did not present with AFP and are therefore not included in the reported paralytic poliomyelitis case count. Between 9 and 20 November 2026, twelve additional AFP cases were reported from several locations in Deir Ez Zor Governorate. Epidemiological and laboratory investigations are ongoing.
Genetic analysis confirmed that the cVDPV1 isolates detected are genetically linked, providing evidence of person-to-person transmission. The event represents a new emergence of cVDPV1. The current emergence is not genetically linked to the VDPV1 previously detected through environmental surveillance at the Al-Mayadin site in February 2026.
Following activation of the Emergency Operations Centre, national health authorities, with support from WHO and partners, are coordinating the outbreak response. Response measures include rapid-response vaccinations, active case finding, strengthened AFP surveillance and reinforcement of routine immunization services, risk communication, and efforts to restore access to essential health services in affected communities.

The next phase must prioritize quality, reach and community trust, alongside sustained funding, coordination and security to save lives and end the outbreak.
On 18 November 2026, the Director-General of WHO, concurring with the advice of the IHR Emergency Committee formulated at its third meeting, on 17 November 2026, determined that the event continues to constitute a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC). after.title: Chikungunya virus disease - Switzerland
after.summary:
On 4 November 2026, health authorities in the canton of Ticino, Switzerland, in coordination with federal authorities, reported four locally acquired cases of chikungunya virus disease. These are the first reported locally acquired chikungunya cases in Switzerland. The earliest reported symptom onset was 10 August 2026, although this infection was identified retrospectively and the source of infection could not be identified. All cases were identified in October 2026. None of the affected individuals reported recent travel to areas with known chikungunya virus transmission, and all four resided in the same geographically defined area. All cases had a favourable clinical course, although joint symptoms persisted in some individuals.

The Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), a competent vector for chikungunya virus, is established in several Swiss cantons, including Ticino. Public health authorities have implemented active case finding, enhanced health care-provider awareness, entomological investigations, targeted vector-control interventions and risk communication. No additional suspected cases were identified through enhanced surveillance and active case finding among health care providers and the two emergency departments serving the affected area.

Based on the currently available information and the seasonal decline in mosquito activity, the risk of further local transmission is considered low. However, the event demonstrates that local chikungunya transmission is possible in Switzerland following introduction of the virus into areas where competent Aedes mosquito populations are established.

On 29 October 2026, the National International Health Regulations (IHR) Focal Point of the State of Qatar notified the World Health Organization (WHO) of two laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East respiratory syndrome (MERS). The cases were confirmed on 5 and 25 August 2026 and are the first MERS cases reported from Qatar since 2022. 

MERS is a viral zoonotic infection, principally transmitted to humans through direct or indirect contact with infected dromedary camels. Both patients were men aged over 50 years with underlying medical conditions and occupational exposure to dromedary camels. Both were hospitalized and subsequently discharged in a stable condition. 

A total of 99 contacts from both cases were identified, tested, and monitored for 14 days following their last exposure. All contacts tested negative for MERS-CoV, and no secondary cases were identified. The two cases reported exposure to dromedary camels at geographically separate farms, with no epidemiological link identified between them. The cases appear to represent sporadic infections associated with zoonotic transmission from dromedary camels rather than human-to-human transmission.

after.summary:
On 20 October 2026, the National IHR Focal Point (NFP) of France notified WHO regarding the first documented human infection with Shamonda virus (SHAV). The case was an immunocompromised older man from eastern France with no travel history during the preceding year. He developed severe neurological illness on 23 September 2026 and was diagnosed with severe encephalitis (brain inflammation). The patient died on 8 October 2026. 
SHAV is recognized primarily as an animal-associated virus, like the closely related Schmallenberg virus circulating in Europe, with no previously documented human infections.
SHAV was confirmed by metagenomic sequencing and reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), with high viral loads detected in tissue samples collected after death and other causes of encephalitis excluded. There is currently widespread SHAV circulation in animals in Europe, including outbreaks across much of France. The source and route of human infection remain unknown. While vector-borne transmission is most likely, food-borne transmission is under investigation. As this is the first documented laboratory confirmed human infection, WHO considers that the public health risk cannot yet be reliably assessed and recommends continued One Health surveillance and investigation.

after.title: Pneumonia of undetermined etiology - the Russian Federation
after.summary:
On 2 October 2026, WHO became aware through media reports of the death of an employee of the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East, the Russian Federation. According to these reports, the individual died on 2 October following hospitalization for severe pneumonia on 29 September, and pneumonic plague was suspected as the cause of death, following occupational exposure in laboratory settings. 
Following requests for verification from WHO, the National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations (2005) (NFP) of the Russian Federation confirmed the death and informed WHO that no case of plague had been registered recently in Irkutsk Oblast, that preventive and control measures had been implemented in accordance with national sanitary legislation, and that the laboratory testing of contacts detected no high-threat pathogens. The authorities also reported that no biosecurity incidents had occurred in the laboratory, contrary to reports in the media, and that there were no further case of severe pneumonia linked to this case. 
The NFP informed WHO that the case and all contacts had been tested for a range of microorganisms, including high-threat pathogens. Test results were negative for the tested high-threat pathogens. All contacts had been medically followed up in healthcare facilities or at home, and all remained asymptomatic throughout. Quarantine measures were instituted in the hospital where the patient was being treated. Based on the information provided by NFP, WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker. 
WHO will continue to monitor the situation and assess any potential public health implications as further information becomes available.

At the national level, transmission remains intense, although the burden is unevenly distributed. In some areas, there are clear signs that the epidemic is slowing down, although in others it continues to grow. Over the past three completed epidemiological weeks, new weekly cases nationwide have increased by 2.5% from 475 to 487, while new weekly deaths remain stable at 224 compared to 222. 

The persistently high mortality, together with the large number of deaths occurring outside treatment centres, continues to point to delays in identifying illness and reaching appropriate care. Since the last Disease Outbreak News, 264 of the 372 reported deaths occurred in communities and 108 in treatment centres. 

On 1 October, the Netherlands reported the medical evacuation of a healthcare worker who tested positive by PCR for Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.  At the time of reporting, the patient has been undergoing treatment in the Netherlands.

Quarantine measures were instituted in the hospital where the patient was being treated. Based on the information provided by NFP, WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. WHO will continue to monitor the situation and assess any potential public health implications as further information becomes available.

On 20 October 2026, the National IHR Focal Point (NFP) of France notified WHO regarding the first documented human infection with Shamonda virus (SHAV). The case was an immunocompromised older man from eastern France with no travel history during the preceding year. He developed severe neurological illness on 23 September 2026 and was diagnosed with severe encephalitis (brain inflammation). The patient died on 8 October 2026. 
SHAV is recognized primarily as an animal-associated virus, like the closely related Schmallenberg virus circulating in Europe, with no previously documented human infections.
SHAV was confirmed by metagenomic sequencing and reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), with high viral loads detected in tissue samples collected after death and other causes of encephalitis excluded. There is currently widespread SHAV circulation in animals in Europe, including outbreaks across much of France. The source and route of human infection remain unknown. While vector-borne transmission is most likely, food-borne transmission is under investigation. As this is the first documented laboratory confirmed human infection, WHO considers that the public health risk cannot yet be reliably assessed and recommends continued One Health surveillance and investigation.

On 2 October 2026, WHO became aware through media reports of the death of an employee of the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute (APRI) of Siberia and the Far East, the Russian Federation. According to these reports, the individual died on 2 October following hospitalization for severe pneumonia on 29 September, and pneumonic plague was suspected as the cause of death, following occupational exposure in laboratory settings. 
Following requests for verification from WHO, the National Focal Point for the International Health Regulations (2005) (NFP) of the Russian Federation confirmed the death and informed WHO that no case of plague had been registered recently in Irkutsk Oblast, that preventive and control measures had been implemented in accordance with national sanitary legislation, and that the laboratory testing of contacts detected no high-threat pathogens. The authorities also reported that no biosecurity incidents had occurred in the laboratory, contrary to reports in the media, and that there were no further case of severe pneumonia linked to this case. 
The NFP informed WHO that the case and all contacts had been tested for a range of microorganisms, including high-threat pathogens. Test results were negative for the tested high-threat pathogens. All contacts had been medically followed up in healthcare facilities or at home, and all remained asymptomatic throughout. Quarantine measures were instituted in the hospital where the patient was being treated. Based on the information provided by NFP, WHO has not identified evidence of ongoing transmission associated with this event. A key uncertainty remains the absence of a confirmed diagnosis in the deceased laboratory worker. 
WHO will continue to monitor the situation and assess any potential public health implications as further information becomes available.

In some areas, there are clear signs that the epidemic is slowing down, although in others it continues to grow. Over the past three completed epidemiological weeks, new weekly cases nationwide have increased by 2.5% from 475 to 487, while new weekly deaths remain stable at 224 compared to 222. 

The persistently high mortality, together with the large number of deaths occurring outside treatment centres, continues to point to delays in identifying illness and reaching appropriate care. Since the last Disease Outbreak News, 264 of the 372 reported deaths occurred in communities and 108 in treatment centres.

Since the last Disease Outbreak News was published on 11 September 2026, the Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded further, with two additional health zones affected. These include Bulu health zone in a new province, Sud Ubangi, located on the north-west part of the country and Dungu health zone in Haut-Uélé province, bordering South Sudan. This brings the total number of affected health zones to 63 across seven provinces out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi and Tshopo. This latest geographic expansion increases the risk of cross-border transmission. 

As of 23 September 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported 7890 confirmed cases, including 3799 deaths, resulting in a crude case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.1%.  

At the national level, the number of new cases reported each day remains high. However, the situation varies across the country, with some provinces and health zones experiencing much higher levels of transmission than others.  

The continuously high CFR, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care. These delays can contribute to preventable illness and deaths among people in affected and newly affected areas, while also allowing transmission to continue within households, communities, and healthcare settings.
